questions.prompt: Milo approached for contact but freezes after several strokes. Which reading is most defensible?

options.text: Her approach remains permission to continue until she actively leaves.
options.feedback: An approach describes the beginning of contact. Freezing can be inhibition, so waiting for a larger refusal ignores the changed signal.

options.text: Pause contact and see whether Milo chooses to lean in, remain still, or move away.
options.feedback: This is the best judgement because it treats consent as continuous and lets Milo's next observable action guide what follows.

options.text: Hold her still briefly so the freeze does not become an avoidance habit.
options.feedback: Restraint adds pressure to an inhibited cat and invents a training problem instead of responding to the signal already present.

questions.prompt: Which group contains an inhibition signal rather than an obvious repelling signal?

options.text: Freezing, half-shut eyes, and ears rotating backwards.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Inhibition can look quiet and is easy to misread as calm if the owner waits only for active resistance.

options.text: Growling, hissing, swatting, and biting.
options.feedback: These are repelling signals. They are important, but the chapter asks owners to notice quieter inhibition before interaction reaches this point.

options.text: Tail up, rubbing, moving closer, and relaxed posture.
options.feedback: These belong to the positive or engaging family. They support contact only while the rest of Milo's signals remain consistent.

questions.prompt: What does Milo's age near the classic sensitive-period boundary mean for handling?

options.text: Her personality is now fixed, so new positive experiences have little value.
options.feedback: The sources do not support a fixed-personality conclusion. Later learning remains possible even though the classic window may be closing.

options.text: Interactions should be frequent, brief, positive, and easy for Milo to leave.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The timing raises the value of careful positive experience without justifying force or rushed exposure.

options.text: She should meet every likely visitor quickly before the window closes completely.
options.feedback: This confuses deliberate exposure with maximum exposure. A rushed or negative first experience can be more harmful than a slower introduction.

questions.prompt: Milo grabs a hand during play. Which response best shapes the future interaction?

options.text: Keep playing because kitten bites are too small to establish a lasting pattern.
options.feedback: The present bite may be small, but continuing pairs hands with the play sequence and allows the handling pattern to become established.

options.text: Redirect the movement onto a wand or other toy and keep hands out of the play target.
options.feedback: This is the best response because it preserves appropriate play while preventing skin from becoming the object Milo practises catching.

options.text: End all play immediately whenever teeth appear so Milo learns play is unsafe.
options.feedback: Stopping pressure may be useful, but removing play entirely misses the constructive option: redirect the same motivation onto an appropriate toy.

questions.prompt: A gentle visitor wants to pick Milo up on their first meeting. What plan best protects Milo's choice?

options.text: Allow it because gentleness makes an unfamiliar person's contact low risk.
options.feedback: Good intention does not transfer the owner's rapport. Milo still needs to approach, engage, and remain able to end contact with this person.

options.text: Have the visitor sit, let Milo approach, and stop if inhibition or avoidance appears.
options.feedback: This is the best plan because it gives the visitor a usable consent-check and keeps the interaction responsive to Milo's current signals.

options.text: Keep Milo separated throughout every visit until she is fully grown.
options.feedback: This prevents forcing but turns temporary caution into blanket isolation. Gradual, cat-led introduction remains possible and useful.

questions.prompt: A child moves quickly toward Milo while a parent is present. What is the strongest owner-level response?

options.text: Ask the parent to enforce one rule: if Milo moves away, contact stops and nobody follows.
options.feedback: This is the best judgement. It turns the principles into a simple enforceable boundary and keeps responsibility with the supervising adult.

options.text: Let the child try once so the adults can see whether Milo is naturally good with children.
options.feedback: This uses Milo as the test and waits for a negative response. A predictable rule should exist before fast movement or reaching begins.

options.text: State that children and cats should never share a room because subtle signals are too difficult.
options.feedback: This over-corrects and is not supported by the sources. Supervision and a concrete stop rule can manage the relevant interaction variables.

questions.prompt: Which weekly plan best combines socialisation timing, consent, play, and cooperative care?

options.text: Schedule long daily handling sessions so Milo becomes accustomed before the sensitive window closes.
options.feedback: The timing concern is real, but long compulsory handling removes the choice and positive pairing that make an experience useful.

options.text: Use brief positive sessions: Milo may approach or leave, play moves to toys, and carrier steps are paired with rewards.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis because it joins timing with cat-led interaction, appropriate play, and gradual cooperative-care practice.

options.text: Avoid planned interaction and wait for Milo to invent every useful handling and carrier experience herself.
options.feedback: Choice matters, but owners still design safe opportunities. Passive waiting does not create the gradual reward-paired practice future care requires.
